screens.title: Real-time Graph Analytics and Event-Driven Architectures
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why Neo4j is a strong fit for real-time analytics and how event-driven architectures supply the live data that keeps graphs actionable. We'll connect the idea of streaming events — such as product views or transactions — to the Cypher MERGE operations that safely update the graph, and we'll show server-side mechanisms like APOC triggers and CDC connectors that let Neo4j both consume and produce events. Real-time graph analytics means you can detect patterns, like suspicious transactions or fast-moving product trends, in milliseconds rather than hours. That matters because timely signals let your application alert users, update recommendations, or block risky activity immediately. You'll also learn important system patterns: designing idempotent consumers, handling eventual consistency, and setting up monitoring and dead-letter queues for failed events. As a concrete orientation, imagine a ProductViewed event published each time a user opens a product page; a small consumer takes that event, runs a MERGE to create or update nodes and a VIEWED relationship, and the graph becomes the live dataset behind a recommendation query. By the end of this module you'll be able to design an event flow into Neo4j, choose between triggers or CDC for your needs, and reason about consistency and errors. Consider now: which event in your system would you want reflected in your graph immediately, and why?

keyIdea.text: Event streams feed Neo4j in real time so graph queries can produce immediate insights; design choices like MERGE, APOC triggers, and CDC tools determine safety, latency, and complexity.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Overview
Real-time Graph Analytics
Harness event streams so graph traversals return instant insights for fraud, recommendations, and supply chain decisions.
In this lesson

Design event flows, update Neo4j with idempotent MERGE operations, react to internal changes with APOC, and stream changes with CDC tools.

Why it matters

Fast, connected queries let applications notify users and block risk before damage spreads. Real-time graphs change system behavior from reactive reporting to proactive response.

Example flow
A ProductViewed event is published, a consumer merges User and Product and a VIEWED relationship, and recommendation queries run on the updated graph within milliseconds.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Streaming Topics
Design, safety, and patterns for graphs that react to events.
Connectors & Tools
APOC triggers, Neo4j Streams, message brokers like Kafka and RabbitMQ.
Patterns & Risks
Idempotency, eventual consistency, error handling, monitoring.
Explore Key Topics
Start by mapping the events you already emit and decide whether Neo4j should be updated immediately by a consumer or via CDC. This choice shapes latency and consistency trade-offs.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide the chapter. First, you'll explain how Neo4j supports real-time graph analytics so you can justify using a graph for fast pattern detection. Second, you'll understand event-driven architecture principles, including how components publish and subscribe to events via message brokers. Third, you'll learn to design an event-driven flow that populates or updates Neo4j — reading an event, constructing an idempotent MERGE-based Cypher query, and committing changes in a transaction. Fourth, you'll explore mechanisms for reacting to changes inside Neo4j, such as APOC triggers and external change data capture tools like the Neo4j Streams connector. Each skill ties to practical uses: for example, detecting fraud from live transaction events, or updating recommendations after a product view. Along the way we will highlight common pitfalls: assuming synchronous consistency across systems, neglecting idempotency, or skipping monitoring. By the end you will be able to propose a concrete consumer design and choose an approach — triggers or CDC — based on your needs and constraints.

screens.title: Real-time Graph Analytics: definition and value
screens.narratorSegment: Real-time graph analytics is the immediate processing and analysis of connected data as it arrives, allowing applications to respond to patterns within milliseconds. In practice this means listening to event streams, updating a graph with those events, and running pattern-matching queries to detect signals such as suspicious transaction chains or rapidly shifting product affinities. A concrete example from fraud detection: two transactions with the same card in distant cities within minutes can form a pattern of concern when linked by shared card, device, or IP nodes; a short Cypher traversal finds the pattern quickly. A common misconception is that real-time means synchronous consistency — it does not. Many architectures accept eventual consistency: the graph will converge as events are processed, and your design must tolerate short windows of divergence. That is why idempotency and retries are crucial: consumers must be safe to run the same event multiple times without duplicating relationships. The takeaway is practical: choose a real-time graph when relationships matter to the query, design your consumer for idempotent merges, and plan for monitoring and recovery so the live graph remains a reliable source of immediate insights. What live signal in your system would you surface first with a real-time graph?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Immediate analysis of connected data to enable fast, relationship-aware decisions such as fraud alerts or live recommendations.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Real-time Graph Analytics
What it is
Immediate processing of events and graph updates to run fast relationship queries.
Why it helps
  • Detect complex patterns across connected entities in milliseconds.
  • Power features like fraud alerts, recommendations, and intrusion detection.
  • Enable richer personalization because relationships are live.
Common misconception
Real-time does not guarantee synchronous consistency across systems; expect eventual consistency and design for it.
Key Takeaway

Use real-time graphs when relationship-aware queries drive behavior; design consumers for idempotency and monitoring to manage consistency trade-offs.

Concrete example: fraud detection
As transactions stream in, create Transaction, Card, Device, and Location nodes and relationships. A short traversal finds suspicious travel or shared devices in seconds.
Analogy
Think of the graph as a whiteboard that is updated live, so pattern-matching queries read the most recent connections instead of stale batch reports.

screens.title: Event-driven architecture basics
screens.narratorSegment: Event-driven architecture is a pattern where components communicate by producing and consuming events, rather than calling each other synchronously. The typical flow begins with an event source that emits events — for example a web front-end publishing ProductViewed or a payment system emitting TransactionCreated. Those events land in a message broker such as Kafka, RabbitMQ, or a cloud queue. Consumers subscribe to relevant topics or queues and process messages asynchronously. When a consumer updates Neo4j it should parse the payload, use a driver to open a transactional session, and run idempotent Cypher that uses MERGE to create or update nodes and relationships. This decouples systems and allows each to scale independently. A practical misconception to avoid is assuming ordering guarantees across unrelated topics; if order matters, design partitioning or sequence fields into the event schema. Another practical detail is consumer retries: transient failures should be retried, persistent failures should land in a dead-letter queue for investigation. The concrete example to keep in mind: a ProductViewed event is published, a consumer uses MERGE to ensure the user and product nodes exist and records a VIEWED relationship with a timestamp, and the updated graph immediately supports similarity queries. How would you partition events to preserve necessary ordering in your domain?

keyIdea.title: Event flow
keyIdea.text: Producers publish events to brokers; consumers read events, run idempotent Cypher in transactions, and update Neo4j asynchronously.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › EDA Flow
Event-driven flow
A clear sequence from event emission to graph update with operational concerns.
1. Event source
Web UI, payment gateway, IoT sensor — emits ProductViewed, TransactionCreated, or SensorReading.
2. Message broker
Kafka, RabbitMQ, or cloud queues buffer and route events to interested consumers.
3. Consumer service
Parses events, ensures idempotency, opens a Neo4j transaction, and runs Cypher MERGE statements.
4. Neo4j graph
Nodes and relationships are created or updated; queries then read the live graph for insights.
Operational notes
  • Use MERGE to achieve idempotency for repeated events.
  • Design retry and dead-letter handling for failures.
  • If ordering matters, partition or include sequence fields in events.

screens.title: Designing an event-driven flow for Neo4j
screens.narratorSegment: Designing an event-driven consumer for Neo4j requires three durable decisions: how you parse events, how you map event fields to graph entities, and how you write Cypher to be idempotent. A widely used pattern is the MERGE-based consumer: on each ProductViewed or UserRegistered event, the consumer opens a transactional session and runs MERGE for the user and the product, then MERGE for the VIEWED relationship, updating timestamps in ON CREATE or ON MATCH clauses. This ensures that repeated delivery of the same event does not create duplicate nodes or extra relationships. The consumer should also validate event payloads, handle schema evolution by ignoring unknown fields or versioning the event contract, and emit metrics for processed, retried, and failed events. A misconception is to treat MERGE as a full substitute for transactional logic; MERGE helps idempotency, but you still need retries, timeouts, and dead-letter handling for persistent failures. As a concrete walkthrough, imagine receiving a ProductViewed event: extract userId and productId, run a MERGE sequence to ensure entities and relationships, commit the transaction, and emit a processed metric. The closing question is: what metrics would you track to know your consumer is healthy and your graph is fresh?

keyIdea.title: Consumer design
keyIdea.text: Parse, map, MERGE, and commit inside a transaction; combine idempotency with monitoring and error handling.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Consumer Design
MERGE-based consumer
A reliable pattern for idempotent updates from events into Neo4j.
Essential steps
  1. Consume event and validate payload.
  2. Open Neo4j transactional session via driver.
  3. Run MERGE statements to create/update nodes and relationships.
  4. Commit and emit metrics; on persistent failure move to dead-letter queue.
Misconception
MERGE helps idempotency but is not a complete failure-handling solution. You still need retries, timeouts, and DLQs for robust pipelines.
Concrete example
// Cypher executed by an event consumer
MERGE (u:User {id: $userId})
MERGE (p:Product {id: $productId})
MERGE (u)-[r:VIEWED]->(p)
ON CREATE SET r.timestamp = datetime()
ON MATCH SET r.timestamp = datetime()
RETURN u, p, r
This sequence ensures users and products are created if missing and the VIEWED relationship is updated with a fresh timestamp so downstream queries observe recent activity.

screens.title: Idempotency and MERGE: example consumer patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Idempotency is the property that allows an operation to be applied multiple times without changing the result beyond the first application. For event consumers this is essential because brokers can redeliver messages. In Neo4j the MERGE clause is a practical tool for idempotency: MERGE either finds an existing pattern or creates it, so repeated runs of the same MERGE sequence do not create duplicate nodes or relationships. A concrete example is a UserRegistered event where a consumer MERGEs a User node by id and sets username and email. A common pitfall is assuming MERGE on relationships behaves the same regardless of additional properties; if you MERGE a relationship including properties, you may inadvertently create multiples. The safer approach is to identify unique keys in nodes and MERGE the nodes, then MERGE the relationship without volatile properties, and set timestamps or counters in ON CREATE / ON MATCH. To ground this idea, the hands-on starter script simulates repeated UserRegistered events where the same user appears with updated fields; the correct consumer uses MERGE so the user's node is updated rather than duplicated. Final question: how will your event schema include unique identifiers so MERGE can be reliable?

keyIdea.title: Idempotency pattern
keyIdea.text: Use MERGE on stable identifiers for nodes and separate property updates into ON CREATE / ON MATCH to avoid duplicates.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Idempotency
MERGE for idempotency
MERGE is the core Cypher tool that avoids duplicate nodes when you have stable keys like userId or productId.
Guidelines
  • MERGE nodes on a unique identifier only.
  • MERGE relationships without volatile properties; set those properties with ON CREATE/ON MATCH.
  • Validate event IDs before running Cypher to avoid creating nodes with missing keys.
Misconception
MERGE eliminates the need for transactional design — incorrect. It helps idempotency but you still need proper commit boundaries and retry logic.
Starter code context
The exercise script simulates repeated UserRegistered events. Implement process_user_registered_event to MERGE the user by id and set username and email.
# Example Cypher pattern to use in a consumer transaction
MERGE (u:User {id: $userId})
SET u.username = $username, u.email = $email
RETURN u
Use this MERGE pattern inside a write transaction so processing repeated events updates properties without creating duplicate User nodes.

screens.title: APOC triggers: reacting from inside Neo4j
screens.narratorSegment: APOC triggers allow Neo4j to react to internal graph events by executing Cypher procedures when nodes or relationships are created, updated, or deleted. They are server-side pieces of logic that run in response to graph activity, which can be used to emit events to external systems or to keep derived data consistent. A typical use is to publish a UserCreated event whenever a new User node is created; the example trigger UNWINDs newly created nodes filtered by label and calls a custom sendEvent procedure to publish to a broker. One misconception is expecting APOC triggers to replace a full CDC strategy: triggers are useful for specific, immediate reactions, but for large-scale, robust change propagation you may prefer a streaming connector like Neo4j Streams to avoid writing many bespoke procedures. Triggers also run inside the database process, so be mindful of performance and error handling: long-running or blocking operations can affect the database. The practical takeaway is that APOC triggers let Neo4j actively participate in an event-driven ecosystem, but use them for targeted reactions and prefer external streaming connectors for broad, durable publication of changes. Would you use triggers for every change in your system or only for a small set of critical events?

keyIdea.title: APOC triggers
keyIdea.text: Server-side callbacks that execute Cypher on graph events; good for targeted reactions but consider scale and performance.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › APOC Triggers
APOC triggers overview
Define server-side procedures that run when nodes or relationships change to publish events or maintain derived data.
Example intent

Publish a UserCreated event whenever a new User node appears so other services can react immediately.

Caveat
Triggers execute inside the DB process; avoid long-running external calls inside triggers to prevent database impact.
Example trigger (conceptual)
CALL apoc.trigger.add(
  'user_created_event',
  'UNWIND apoc.trigger.nodesByLabel($createdNodes, "User") AS n '
  + 'WITH n CALL apoc.custom.sendEvent("user_created", {userId: n.id, username: n.username}) YIELD value RETURN value',
  {phase:'after'}
)
This trigger selects newly created User nodes and delegates publishing to a custom procedure. For wide distribution prefer a streaming connector.

screens.title: Change Data Capture (CDC) and Neo4j Streams
screens.narratorSegment: Change Data Capture is an architectural approach for tracking and streaming the changes that happen to your data so other systems can react. For Neo4j, CDC often takes the form of a connector such as Neo4j Streams that pushes graph updates to brokers like Kafka, enabling downstream consumers to see node and relationship changes without polling the database. CDC is attractive when you need reliable, broad propagation of every change, or when maintaining many custom triggers would be burdensome. Compared to APOC triggers, CDC connectors are designed for scale and integration: they capture a stream of changes and preserve ordering and metadata in a broker-friendly format. A common misconception is that CDC eliminates the need for idempotency downstream — it does not. Consumers of CDC streams still must be idempotent because connectors can replay messages. When to prefer CDC over triggers depends on scope: use triggers for a small set of immediate reactions, and use CDC for system-wide change streaming and integration with analytics, search indexing, or archival pipelines. The final reflection: what systems in your landscape should subscribe to a CDC stream coming out of Neo4j?

keyIdea.title: CDC idea
keyIdea.text: Stream graph changes to message brokers so many consumers can react without polling the database or writing many bespoke triggers.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › CDC & Streams
Change Data Capture
Capture and publish every data change so other systems can subscribe without polling.
When to use CDC
  • When many downstream systems need a durable stream of changes.
  • When you want a single integration point rather than many custom triggers.
Misconception
CDC removes the need for downstream idempotency or retry logic — it does not. Consumers must still handle duplicates and ordering as required.
Practical note
Neo4j Streams can connect Neo4j to Kafka so graph changes are published as events. Use this for broad integration, analytics, search indexing, or replication workflows.
Key Takeaway

Choose CDC when you need a durable, system-wide stream of graph changes; choose triggers for isolated, immediate reactions.

screens.title: Real-time recommendations: an end-to-end example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a focused example: turning ProductViewed events into real-time recommendations. When a user views a product, the front-end publishes a ProductViewed event containing userId, productId, and timestamp. A consumer subscribed to that topic parses the event and runs MERGE to ensure both the User and Product nodes exist, then MERGE to create or update a VIEWED relationship with the latest timestamp. As many events accumulate, the graph builds a dense network of user-product interactions that can be queried to find users with similar viewing patterns, frequently co-viewed products, or hot items for a cohort. A key point is that the Cypher queries that produce recommendations are often short traversals — they read relationships rather than perform expensive joins across many tables. A misconception is assuming recommendation quality comes only from volume; the richness of relationships and the freshness of edges matter more for contextual suggestions. Operationally, you must include idempotency in the consumer, metrics to measure freshness, and a dead-letter queue to capture malformed events. For reflection: which similarity query would be most valuable in your product catalog and what freshness window would you require for recommendations to feel real-time?

screens.title: Handling failures: retries and dead-letter queues
screens.narratorSegment: Errors are inevitable in an event-driven pipeline. The recommended approach is a two-tiered handling strategy: retry transient failures automatically and send persistent or unparseable messages to a dead-letter queue for manual inspection. For example, network blips between the consumer and Neo4j should trigger a bounded retry policy with exponential backoff; if retries fail, the consumer pushes the event into a DLQ with context and metrics. Idempotent operations reduce the risk of inconsistent results across retries, because reprocessing the same MERGE statements will not create duplicates. Track metrics such as processed, retried, and failed counts, plus consumer lag and the age of the oldest unprocessed event; these help you detect backlogs and data freshness issues. A misconception is to retry indefinitely without escalation — that hides persistent bugs and delays remediation. Instead, configure a reasonable retry window and surface failed events quickly to a team with a reproducible payload and error logs. The practical question to consider is: what retry policy and DLQ retention will meet your business SLAs while keeping the pipeline observable and debuggable? screens.title: Operational monitoring for real-time graphs
screens.narratorSegment: Operational monitoring keeps a real-time graph trustworthy. Key metrics include consumer lag (how far behind the consumer is relative to the head of the topic), age of the oldest unprocessed event, number of processed, retried, and failed events, DLQ size and growth rate, database transaction latency, and query latency for your most critical read patterns. Instrument counters and histograms for these metrics and create alerts on thresholds relevant to your SLA: for example, consumer lag exceeding a minute or DLQ growth beyond an expected baseline. A misconception is relying solely on database uptime; uptime does not imply your graph is fresh. In addition to metrics, include periodic consistency checks: sample recent events and verify corresponding nodes and relationships exist in the graph. Finally, add logging with event ids and correlation ids so failed payloads can be replayed or diagnosed. The practical question for you is: what alert thresholds make sense given how recent your graph must be for customer-facing features? fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why Neo4j is a strong fit for real-time analytics and how event-driven architectures supply the live data that keeps graphs actionable. We'll connect the idea of streaming events — such as product views or transactions — to the Cypher MERGE operations that safely update the graph, and we'll show server-side mechanisms like APOC triggers and CDC connectors that let Neo4j both consume and produce events. Real-time graph analytics means you can detect patterns, like suspicious transactions or fast-moving product trends, in milliseconds rather than hours. That matters because timely signals let your application alert users, update recommendations, or block risky activity immediately. You'll also learn important system patterns: designing idempotent consumers, handling eventual consistency, and setting up monitoring and dead-letter queues for failed events. As a concrete orientation, imagine a ProductViewed event published each time a user opens a product page; a small consumer takes that event, runs a MERGE to create or update nodes and a VIEWED relationship, and the graph becomes the live dataset behind a recommendation query. By the end of this module you'll be able to design an event flow into Neo4j, choose between triggers or CDC for your needs, and reason about consistency and errors. Consider now: which event in your system would you want reflected in your graph immediately, and why?

These objectives guide the chapter. First, you'll explain how Neo4j supports real-time graph analytics so you can justify using a graph for fast pattern detection. Second, you'll understand event-driven architecture principles, including how components publish and subscribe to events via message brokers. Third, you'll learn to design an event-driven flow that populates or updates Neo4j — reading an event, constructing an idempotent MERGE-based Cypher query, and committing changes in a transaction. Fourth, you'll explore mechanisms for reacting to changes inside Neo4j, such as APOC triggers and external change data capture tools like the Neo4j Streams connector. Each skill ties to practical uses: for example, detecting fraud from live transaction events, or updating recommendations after a product view. Along the way we will highlight common pitfalls: assuming synchronous consistency across systems, neglecting idempotency, or skipping monitoring. By the end you will be able to propose a concrete consumer design and choose an approach — triggers or CDC — based on your needs and constraints.

This page continues the objectives with a focus on tools and system-level trade-offs. First, you will learn how message brokers and event consumers work together, including the role brokers play in decoupling producers and consumers. Second, you will practice writing idempotent consumer logic — ensuring repeated delivery of the same event doesn't create duplicate nodes or relationships by relying on MERGE and careful transaction boundaries. Third, you'll explore Change Data Capture patterns and the Neo4j Streams style connector that streams graph changes to brokers like Kafka when you need broad propagation. Fourth, you will identify common patterns and challenges: eventual consistency between services, designing retry and dead-letter mechanisms, and monitoring the freshness of your graph. Each card includes a small mnemonic to help you recall the skill and a verified milestone so you know when you have demonstrated competence. These skills let you plan a safe, scalable pipeline from events to a live recommendation or fraud detection dataset.

Real-time graph analytics is the immediate processing and analysis of connected data as it arrives, allowing applications to respond to patterns within milliseconds. In practice this means listening to event streams, updating a graph with those events, and running pattern-matching queries to detect signals such as suspicious transaction chains or rapidly shifting product affinities. A concrete example from fraud detection: two transactions with the same card in distant cities within minutes can form a pattern of concern when linked by shared card, device, or IP nodes; a short Cypher traversal finds the pattern quickly. A common misconception is that real-time means synchronous consistency — it does not. Many architectures accept eventual consistency: the graph will converge as events are processed, and your design must tolerate short windows of divergence. That is why idempotency and retries are crucial: consumers must be safe to run the same event multiple times without duplicating relationships. The takeaway is practical: choose a real-time graph when relationships matter to the query, design your consumer for idempotent merges, and plan for monitoring and recovery so the live graph remains a reliable source of immediate insights. What live signal in your system would you surface first with a real-time graph?

Event-driven architecture is a pattern where components communicate by producing and consuming events, rather than calling each other synchronously. The typical flow begins with an event source that emits events — for example a web front-end publishing ProductViewed or a payment system emitting TransactionCreated. Those events land in a message broker such as Kafka, RabbitMQ, or a cloud queue. Consumers subscribe to relevant topics or queues and process messages asynchronously. When a consumer updates Neo4j it should parse the payload, use a driver to open a transactional session, and run idempotent Cypher that uses MERGE to create or update nodes and relationships. This decouples systems and allows each to scale independently. A practical misconception to avoid is assuming ordering guarantees across unrelated topics; if order matters, design partitioning or sequence fields into the event schema. Another practical detail is consumer retries: transient failures should be retried, persistent failures should land in a dead-letter queue for investigation. The concrete example to keep in mind: a ProductViewed event is published, a consumer uses MERGE to ensure the user and product nodes exist and records a VIEWED relationship with a timestamp, and the updated graph immediately supports similarity queries. How would you partition events to preserve necessary ordering in your domain?

Designing an event-driven consumer for Neo4j requires three durable decisions: how you parse events, how you map event fields to graph entities, and how you write Cypher to be idempotent. A widely used pattern is the MERGE-based consumer: on each ProductViewed or UserRegistered event, the consumer opens a transactional session and runs MERGE for the user and the product, then MERGE for the VIEWED relationship, updating timestamps in ON CREATE or ON MATCH clauses. This ensures that repeated delivery of the same event does not create duplicate nodes or extra relationships. The consumer should also validate event payloads, handle schema evolution by ignoring unknown fields or versioning the event contract, and emit metrics for processed, retried, and failed events. A misconception is to treat MERGE as a full substitute for transactional logic; MERGE helps idempotency, but you still need retries, timeouts, and dead-letter handling for persistent failures. As a concrete walkthrough, imagine receiving a ProductViewed event: extract userId and productId, run a MERGE sequence to ensure entities and relationships, commit the transaction, and emit a processed metric. The closing question is: what metrics would you track to know your consumer is healthy and your graph is fresh?

Idempotency is the property that allows an operation to be applied multiple times without changing the result beyond the first application. For event consumers this is essential because brokers can redeliver messages. In Neo4j the MERGE clause is a practical tool for idempotency: MERGE either finds an existing pattern or creates it, so repeated runs of the same MERGE sequence do not create duplicate nodes or relationships. A concrete example is a UserRegistered event where a consumer MERGEs a User node by id and sets username and email. A common pitfall is assuming MERGE on relationships behaves the same regardless of additional properties; if you MERGE a relationship including properties, you may inadvertently create multiples. The safer approach is to identify unique keys in nodes and MERGE the nodes, then MERGE the relationship without volatile properties, and set timestamps or counters in ON CREATE / ON MATCH. To ground this idea, the hands-on starter script simulates repeated UserRegistered events where the same user appears with updated fields; the correct consumer uses MERGE so the user's node is updated rather than duplicated. Final question: how will your event schema include unique identifiers so MERGE can be reliable?

APOC triggers allow Neo4j to react to internal graph events by executing Cypher procedures when nodes or relationships are created, updated, or deleted. They are server-side pieces of logic that run in response to graph activity, which can be used to emit events to external systems or to keep derived data consistent. A typical use is to publish a UserCreated event whenever a new User node is created; the example trigger UNWINDs newly created nodes filtered by label and calls a custom sendEvent procedure to publish to a broker. One misconception is expecting APOC triggers to replace a full CDC strategy: triggers are useful for specific, immediate reactions, but for large-scale, robust change propagation you may prefer a streaming connector like Neo4j Streams to avoid writing many bespoke procedures. Triggers also run inside the database process, so be mindful of performance and error handling: long-running or blocking operations can affect the database. The practical takeaway is that APOC triggers let Neo4j actively participate in an event-driven ecosystem, but use them for targeted reactions and prefer external streaming connectors for broad, durable publication of changes. Would you use triggers for every change in your system or only for a small set of critical events?

Change Data Capture is an architectural approach for tracking and streaming the changes that happen to your data so other systems can react. For Neo4j, CDC often takes the form of a connector such as Neo4j Streams that pushes graph updates to brokers like Kafka, enabling downstream consumers to see node and relationship changes without polling the database. CDC is attractive when you need reliable, broad propagation of every change, or when maintaining many custom triggers would be burdensome. Compared to APOC triggers, CDC connectors are designed for scale and integration: they capture a stream of changes and preserve ordering and metadata in a broker-friendly format. A common misconception is that CDC eliminates the need for idempotency downstream — it does not. Consumers of CDC streams still must be idempotent because connectors can replay messages. When to prefer CDC over triggers depends on scope: use triggers for a small set of immediate reactions, and use CDC for system-wide change streaming and integration with analytics, search indexing, or archival pipelines. The final reflection: what systems in your landscape should subscribe to a CDC stream coming out of Neo4j?

Let's walk through a focused example: turning ProductViewed events into real-time recommendations. When a user views a product, the front-end publishes a ProductViewed event containing userId, productId, and timestamp.
